title: How to Choose a Local Partner in Thailand: 5 Questions to Ask Before You Sign
excerpt: Not all local partners are equal. Before you commit to a market entry partnership in Thailand, these five questions will tell you everything you need to know.
contentHtml:
The Partner Question No One Asks Until It's Too Late

Most international brands entering Thailand focus on the wrong things. They spend weeks comparing legal structures, debating registration timelines, and evaluating distribution models. Then they sign a partnership agreement with someone they've met twice — and spend the next year managing the consequences.

Choosing a local partner is the single highest-leverage decision in your Thailand market entry. The right partner compresses your timeline from 12 months to 8 weeks. The wrong one turns a $50,000 market test into a $150,000 write-off.

Here are the five questions that separate real operating partners from well-connected consultants.

1. Do you operate, or do you advise?

This is the first and most important question. There are two fundamentally different types of local partners in Thailand: operators and advisors.

Advisors give you strategy, introductions and market maps. They work on retainer, charge for hours, and their income is not connected to your results. When things don't work out, they move on to the next client.

Operators run things. They have infrastructure — kitchens, offices, warehouses, delivery accounts, commercial teams. When your brand fails, they feel it. When it succeeds, they grow with you.

The question to ask: Show me something you are currently operating. If they cannot point to a running business, you have an advisor, not an operator.

2. What's already live and ready to use on day one?

Every local partner will tell you they can set up the infrastructure you need. The right question is: what's already running?

  • Is there a cloud kitchen already producing for other brands?
  • Are there active accounts on GrabFood, Foodpanda and LINE MAN?
  • Is there a local commercial team already calling accounts?
  • Is there an office where your brand can be represented today?

    • The difference between "we can set this up" and "it's already live" is typically 3 to 6 months. In a fast-moving market like Bangkok, that's the difference between a successful pilot and a missed window.

    3. How is your compensation structured?

    A partner's incentive structure tells you everything about how they'll behave when the market gets difficult — which it always does at some point.

    There are four common models:

  • **Fixed retainer**: Partner earns regardless of results. Risk: they deprioritise your brand when a bigger client comes along.
  • **Commission on sales**: Partner earns only when you sell. Risk: they push for short-term volume over sustainable brand building.
  • **Revenue share**: Partner earns a percentage of top-line revenue. Best alignment for early-stage market entry.
  • **Equity participation**: Partner has skin in the game at the company level. Strongest alignment, appropriate for serious long-term commitments.

    • The best local partners for market entry typically propose a revenue share or performance-based model. If a partner insists on a fixed retainer with no performance component, ask why.

    4. Can you introduce me to a brand you've worked with in the last 12 months?

    References are the most underused due diligence tool in market entry. Every serious operating partner should be able to give you two or three direct introductions to founders they've worked with recently.

    When you speak with references, ask:

  • Did they deliver what they promised, and on what timeline?
  • How did they handle problems when things didn't go as planned?
  • Would you work with them again for a larger commitment?

    • If a partner hesitates to provide references, or only offers testimonials they've written themselves, that's a material signal.

    5. What happens if we need to exit or pivot after 90 days?

    This is the question most brands skip because they don't want to think about failure before they've even started. It's also the question that protects you most.

    A good local partner will have a clear, fair answer. They'll explain what you own, what they own, what the notice period is, and how operational assets are handled if the engagement ends.

    If a partner gets defensive or vague when you ask about exit terms, it means the exit will be expensive and complicated. Build exit terms into the agreement before you sign anything.

    What This Means for Your Decision

    The right local partner for your Thailand entry should be able to answer all five questions clearly and confidently. They should have something already running, a compensation model aligned with your results, recent references, and a fair exit structure.
